Evaluating Heat Adaptation Interventions A Hands-On Workshop: Case-Crossover, Difference-in-Differences, and Inverse Probability Weighting Welcome

Evaluating Heat Adaptation Interventions A Hands-On Workshop: Case-Crossover, Difference-in-Differences, and Inverse Probability Weighting Dr. Amruta Nori-Sarma 2026-08-13 Welcome (About 5 minutes) A note on the data before we start. Everything in this workshop is simulated. It is built to loosely resemble the scale and population characteristics reported in the PRIME-Boston Boston Emergency Services Team (BEST) papers (roughly 6,500 to 8,200 psychiatric ED encounters per warm season, a population that is predominantly publicly insured or uninsured, individually geocoded and linked to gridded ambient temperature), but the specific counts, effect sizes, and the “true” intervention effect below are all invented for teaching purposes. Nothing here is a re-analysis of real BEST data, and nothing here should be read as an estimate of whether any real intervention worked. The point of the exercise is methodological: we know the ground truth we built into the simulation, so we can watch each design either recover it or fail to. Learning objectives. By the end of this workshop you will be able to: Build a synthetic person-day dataset with realistic structure: a daily heat exposure series, drifting population composition, a secular trend, and a known intervention effect. Implement a time-stratified case-crossover analysis and explain what it does and does not control for. Implement a difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis through a reusable model_generalized() function, and build a proper event-study plot with year-by-year estimates relative to the intervention. Build inverse probability weights to address compositional drift in a pre/post comparison, and feed them into the same model_generalized() function used for the DiD estimate. Compare all three estimates against the known ground truth and discuss which assumptions each design leans on, tying back to the critique of the Ahmedabad HAP evaluation. Setup. Run this once before the workshop. If you don’t already have these packages, uncomment the install line. # install.packages(c("bookdown", "dplyr", "tidyr", "tibble", "lubridate", # "survival", "MASS", "timeDate", "ggplot2", "broom")) library(lubridate) library(survival) # clogit() for the case-crossover library(MASS) # kept for the namespace-collision note below (not otherwise used) library(timeDate) # holiday() for the DiD models' holiday flag library(tidyr) # pivot_wider() / unite() library(ggplot2) library(broom) # tidy() for clean model summaries library(dplyr) # loaded LAST on purpose, see note below set.seed(2026) A namespace note, since it trips people up constantly. MASS exports its own select() function (for stepwise model selection), completely unrelated to dplyr::select(). Whichever package you library() last wins any naming collision, so if you load MASS after dplyr, every select(...) call in your script silently starts calling MASS::select() instead, and you’ll get a confusing unused arguments error the moment you try to pick columns. Loading dplyr last (as above) fixes it, but the safest habit is to just write dplyr::select() explicitly anywhere it matters, which is what we do below.

method-1-time-stratified-case-crossover-10-min.html
2 Method 1: Time-Stratified Case-Crossover (10 min)

2 Method 1: Time-Stratified Case-Crossover (10 min) Each case (an encounter) is matched to a handful of control days: same person’s location, same calendar month and year, same day of week as the case day, excluding the case day itself. Because each person is compared only to their own control days, this design controls for anything that is constant for that person and stratum by design (age, insurance, chronic illness, neighborhood). It does not control for a citywide secular trend across the full study period, because that trend operates just as much on the control days as the case day within a given month. To keep runtimes reasonable in a workshop setting, we subsample cases rather than using all ~75,000+ simulated encounters. Feel free to raise n_cases_per_period and rerun at home. n_cases_per_period <- 800 pre_cases <- encounters %>% filter(post == 0) %>% slice_sample(n = n_cases_per_period) post_cases <- encounters %>% filter(post == 1) %>% slice_sample(n = n_cases_per_period) sampled_cases <- bind_rows(pre_cases, post_cases) # lookup table of city-wide daily exposure, used for both case and control days temp_lookup <- daily_df %>% dplyr::select(date, temp, extreme) get_control_days <- function(case_date, n_controls = 4) { same_month <- format(case_date, "%Y-%m") candidates <- temp_lookup %>% filter(format(date, "%Y-%m") == same_month, wday(date) == wday(case_date), date != case_date) if (nrow(candidates) > n_controls) { candidates <- candidates %>% slice_sample(n = n_controls) } candidates } build_cc_dataset <- function(cases_df) { out <- vector("list", nrow(cases_df)) for (i in seq_len(nrow(cases_df))) { case_row <- cases_df[i, ] controls <- get_control_days(case_row$date) if (nrow(controls) == 0) next case_line <- data.frame( strat_id = case_row$id, case = 1, temp = case_row$temp, extreme = case_row$extreme ) control_lines <- data.frame( strat_id = case_row$id, case = 0, temp = controls$temp, extreme = controls$extreme ) out[[i]] <- bind_rows(case_line, control_lines) } bind_rows(out) } cc_pre <- build_cc_dataset(pre_cases) cc_post <- build_cc_dataset(post_cases) cat("Pre-period case-crossover rows:", nrow(cc_pre), "\n") ## Pre-period case-crossover rows: 3540 cat("Post-period case-crossover rows:", nrow(cc_post), "\n") ## Post-period case-crossover rows: 3535 cc_model_pre <- clogit(case ~ extreme + strata(strat_id), data = cc_pre) cc_model_post <- clogit(case ~ extreme + strata(strat_id), data = cc_post) cc_summary <- bind_rows( tidy(cc_model_pre, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>% mutate(period = "Pre (2010-2015)"), tidy(cc_model_post, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>% mutate(period = "Post (2016-2020)") ) %>% filter(term == "extreme") %>% select(period, OR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) print(cc_summary) ## # A tibble: 2 × 5 ## period OR conf.low conf.high p.value ## <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 Pre (2010-2015) 1.65 1.28 2.13 0.000132 ## 2 Post (2016-2020) 1.23 0.945 1.60 0.124 What this does and does not tell us. Comparing the pre-period OR to the post-period OR gives an informal before/after signal, similar in spirit to comparing Ahmedabad’s pre-HAP and post-HAP relative risks. But notice that we have not formally tested whether the two ORs differ from each other, and the case-crossover design by itself has no mechanism for netting out a citywide secular trend that shifted between the two multi- year windows. That’s exactly the gap the next method is built to close.

3 Method 2: Difference-in-Differences (12 min) 3.1 2.1 Descriptive Table 1, with a naive DiD term 3.2 2.2 Event-study plot 3.3 2.3 Poisson regression via model_generalized()

3 Method 2: Difference-in-Differences (12 min) This section follows a three-step DiD pipeline: a descriptive “Table 1” style pre/post comparison with a naive percentage-based DiD term, an event-study plot with a proper event-time regression, and then the formal Poisson regression, run through a reusable model_generalized() function. # a few extra day-level covariates the models below expect: day of week, # week number, and a simple summer holiday flag holiday_years <- 2010:2020 holidays <- c( as.Date(timeDate::holiday(holiday_years, "USMemorialDay")), as.Date(timeDate::holiday(holiday_years, "USIndependenceDay")), as.Date(timeDate::holiday(holiday_years, "USLaborDay")) ) daily_counts <- encounters %>% count(date, name = "n_encounters_actual") %>% right_join(daily_df, by = "date") %>% mutate( n_encounters_actual = ifelse(is.na(n_encounters_actual), 0, n_encounters_actual), dow = wday(date), week = week(date), holid = as.integer(date %in% holidays) ) 3.1 2.1 Descriptive Table 1, with a naive DiD term Compute each group’s share of its own period’s total, take pre-to-post differences within the extreme and non-extreme groups separately, then difference those two differences, a quick sanity check to run before turning to any regression model. pre_total <- sum(daily_counts$n_encounters_actual[daily_counts$post == 0]) post_total <- sum(daily_counts$n_encounters_actual[daily_counts$post == 1]) did_table1 <- daily_counts %>% mutate(extreme_chr = ifelse(extreme == 1, ">= 90th pctile", "< 90th pctile"), post_chr = ifelse(post == 1, "Post", "Pre")) %>% group_by(extreme_chr, post_chr) %>% summarise(visits = sum(n_encounters_actual), .groups = "drop") %>% tidyr::unite("group", extreme_chr, post_chr, sep = " ") %>% tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = visits) did_table1 <- did_table1 %>% mutate( `< 90th pctile Pre (%)` = round(100 * `< 90th pctile Pre` / pre_total, 1), `< 90th pctile Post (%)` = round(100 * `< 90th pctile Post` / post_total, 1), `>= 90th pctile Pre (%)` = round(100 * `>= 90th pctile Pre` / pre_total, 1), `>= 90th pctile Post (%)` = round(100 * `>= 90th pctile Post` / post_total, 1), `< 90th pctile Diff` = `< 90th pctile Post (%)` - `< 90th pctile Pre (%)`, `>= 90th pctile Diff` = `>= 90th pctile Post (%)` - `>= 90th pctile Pre (%)`, `DiD Term` = `< 90th pctile Diff` - `>= 90th pctile Diff` ) print(did_table1, width = Inf) ## # A tibble: 1 × 11 ## `< 90th pctile Post` `< 90th pctile Pre` `>= 90th pctile Post` `>= 90th pctile Pre` ## <int> <int> <int> <int> ## 1 40988 43993 4860 7383 ## `< 90th pctile Pre (%)` `< 90th pctile Post (%)` `>= 90th pctile Pre (%)` `>= 90th pctile Post (%)` ## <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 85.6 89.4 14.4 10.6 ## `< 90th pctile Diff` `>= 90th pctile Diff` `DiD Term` ## <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 3.80 -3.8 7.60 3.2 2.2 Event-study plot A proper event-study design: a Poisson regression with the extreme-heat indicator interacted with a full set of year-relative-to-intervention dummies (event time), so each year gets its own estimated heat effect relative to the year immediately before the intervention (event time -1, the omitted reference category), rather than just comparing raw annual means. event_study_plot <- function(dataframe, outcome_variable, threshold_temp, intervention_year, start_year, end_year) { data <- dataframe %>% filter(year %in% start_year:end_year) %>% mutate(event_time = year - intervention_year) list_event_times <- as.character(seq(min(data$event_time), max(data$event_time))) list_event_times <- c("-1", list_event_times[list_event_times != "-1"]) data <- data %>% mutate(event_time_factor = factor(event_time, levels = list_event_times)) data$outcome_variable <- data[[outcome_variable]] data$threshold_temp <- data[[threshold_temp]] event_model <- glm( outcome_variable ~ threshold_temp + (threshold_temp:event_time_factor) + event_time_factor + holid + year + dow + month + week, data = data, family = poisson ) coefficients <- coef(event_model) interaction_coefficient <- coefficients[grep("threshold_temp:event_time_factor", names(coefficients))] conf_intervals <- confint(event_model) interaction_confint <- conf_intervals[grep("threshold_temp:event_time_factor", rownames(conf_intervals)), ] plot_data <- data.frame(cbind(interaction_coefficient, interaction_confint)) %>% tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "EventTime") plot_data$EventTime <- as.numeric(sub("^threshold_temp:event_time_factor", "", plot_data$EventTime)) plot_data$interaction_coefficient <- exp(plot_data$interaction_coefficient) plot_data$lowCI <- exp(plot_data$X2.5..) plot_data$uppCI <- exp(plot_data$X97.5..) new_row <- data.frame(EventTime = -1, interaction_coefficient = 1, lowCI = 1, uppCI = 1) plot_data <- plot_data %>% dplyr::select(-c(X2.5.., X97.5..)) plot_data2 <- rbind(plot_data, new_row) ggplot(plot_data2, aes(EventTime, interaction_coefficient)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lowCI, ymax = uppCI)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "#A51C30", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, color = "grey") + xlab("Time to intervention (years)") + ylab("Estimated heat effect, relative to year -1") + theme_minimal() + scale_x_continuous( breaks = min(plot_data2$EventTime):max(plot_data2$EventTime), labels = as.character(min(plot_data2$EventTime):max(plot_data2$EventTime)) ) } event_study_plot( dataframe = daily_counts, outcome_variable = "n_encounters_actual", threshold_temp = "extreme", intervention_year = 2016, start_year = 2010, end_year = 2020 ) Reading the plot. Each point is a year’s estimated multiplicative effect of an extreme heat day on encounter counts, relative to the year right before the intervention. If the intervention worked, you’d expect the post-intervention points (event time >= 0) to sit visibly lower than the pre-intervention points. Flat, overlapping confidence intervals across the dashed line, on the other hand, look a lot like the pattern Hess et al. found when they tested whether Ahmedabad’s effect held up without the anomalous 2010 heat wave in the baseline. 3.3 2.3 Poisson regression via model_generalized() A reusable function for the main DiD estimate: a Poisson regression of the outcome on exposure, intervention period, their interaction, and day of week, week, month, year, and a holiday flag, returning the interaction term as an incidence rate ratio with its 95% profile-likelihood confidence interval. model_generalized <- function(dataframe, outcome_count, exposure, intervention, weights = NULL) { if (is.null(weights)) { model <- glm( outcome_count ~ exposure + intervention + (exposure:intervention) + year + holid + month + week + dow, data = dataframe, family = poisson ) } else { model <- glm( outcome_count ~ exposure + intervention + (exposure:intervention) + year + holid + month + week + dow, data = dataframe, family = quasipoisson, weights = weights ) } coefficients <- coef(model) interaction_coefficient <- exp(coefficients[grep("exposure:intervention", names(coefficients))]) conf_intervals <- exp(confint(model)) interaction_confint <- conf_intervals[grep("exposure:intervention", rownames(conf_intervals)), ] paste0(round(interaction_coefficient, 2), " (", round(interaction_confint[1], 2), ", ", round(interaction_confint[2], 2), ")") } Overall model: did_overall_irr <- model_generalized( dataframe = daily_counts, outcome_count = daily_counts$n_encounters_actual, exposure = daily_counts$extreme, intervention = daily_counts$post ) did_overall_irr ## [1] "0.96 (0.92, 1)" Stratified calls, applied to a couple of subgroups the way an actual stratified analysis would: insurance type and chronic mental illness status, since those are the two characteristics with drifting composition built into the simulation. daily_by_group <- function(filter_expr) { encounters %>% filter({{ filter_expr }}) %>% count(date, name = "n_encounters_actual") %>% right_join(daily_df, by = "date") %>% mutate( n_encounters_actual = ifelse(is.na(n_encounters_actual), 0, n_encounters_actual), dow = wday(date), week = week(date), holid = as.integer(date %in% holidays) ) } medicaid_uninsured <- daily_by_group(insurance %in% c("Medicaid", "Uninsured")) commercial_medicare <- daily_by_group(insurance %in% c("Commercial", "Medicare")) chronic_mi_group <- daily_by_group(chronic_mi == 1) data.frame( subgroup = c("Medicaid/Uninsured", "Commercial/Medicare", "Chronic mental illness"), IRR = c( model_generalized(medicaid_uninsured, medicaid_uninsured$n_encounters_actual, medicaid_uninsured$extreme, medicaid_uninsured$post), model_generalized(commercial_medicare, commercial_medicare$n_encounters_actual, commercial_medicare$extreme, commercial_medicare$post), model_generalized(chronic_mi_group, chronic_mi_group$n_encounters_actual, chronic_mi_group$extreme, chronic_mi_group$post) ) ) ## subgroup IRR ## 1 Medicaid/Uninsured 0.97 (0.93, 1.01) ## 2 Commercial/Medicare 0.91 (0.83, 0.99) ## 3 Chronic mental illness 0.99 (0.92, 1.06) Reading the output. The interaction-term IRR is the DiD estimate: a value below 1 means the extra risk on an extreme heat day was smaller after the intervention than before it, controlling for day of week, week, month, year, and holidays. Because we built a true attenuation of about 36% into the simulation, a well-specified DiD model should land somewhere in that neighborhood for the overall estimate.
method-3-inverse-probability-weighting-for-prepost-comparison-8-min.html
4 Method 3: Inverse Probability Weighting for Pre/Post Comparison (8 min)

4 Method 3: Inverse Probability Weighting for Pre/Post Comparison (8 min) The DiD model above still assumes the population being served didn’t change in ways that matter. But we built in exactly the kind of compositional drift Hess et al. flagged as an unmeasured concern for Ahmedabad: rising Medicaid/uninsured share, rising chronic mental illness prevalence, rising social vulnerability. If those shifts are themselves associated with heat sensitivity, they could bias the DiD estimate in either direction. The IPW approach: model the probability that a given encounter falls in the post-period as a function of its measured characteristics, then reweight each day’s contribution to the model so that the weighted population looks similar across the pre- and post-periods on those measured characteristics. This does not fix confounding by unmeasured factors (air pollution, healthcare access, publicity effects) any more than the original Ahmedabad study could, but it does directly address the one confounding pathway we actually simulated and can observe. ps_model <- glm( post ~ age + sex + insurance + chronic_mi + svi, data = encounters, family = binomial ) encounters$p_post <- predict(ps_model, type = "response") marginal_p_post <- mean(encounters$post) encounters <- encounters %>% mutate( sw = ifelse(post == 1, marginal_p_post / p_post, (1 - marginal_p_post) / (1 - p_post)) ) # trim extreme weights, standard practice to avoid a small number of # observations dominating the model sw_caps <- quantile(encounters$sw, c(0.01, 0.99)) encounters$sw_trimmed <- pmin(pmax(encounters$sw, sw_caps[1]), sw_caps[2]) summary(encounters$sw_trimmed) ## Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. ## 0.6386 0.8163 0.9417 0.9973 1.1160 1.9276 # quick covariate balance check: unweighted vs weighted mean SVI and # chronic_mi by period. If weighting is doing its job, the weighted # pre/post gap should shrink relative to the unweighted gap. balance_check <- encounters %>% group_by(post) %>% summarise( unweighted_svi = mean(svi), weighted_svi = weighted.mean(svi, sw_trimmed), unweighted_chronic_mi = mean(chronic_mi), weighted_chronic_mi = weighted.mean(chronic_mi, sw_trimmed) ) print(balance_check) ## # A tibble: 2 × 5 ## post unweighted_svi weighted_svi unweighted_chronic_mi weighted_chronic_mi ## <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 0 0.476 0.501 0.297 0.311 ## 2 1 0.530 0.503 0.328 0.312 # aggregate the per-encounter weights up to a day-level average weight, # then refeed the SAME model_generalized() function used for the DiD # section, now with weights supplied day_weights <- encounters %>% group_by(date) %>% summarise(day_avg_sw = mean(sw_trimmed)) daily_counts_ipw <- daily_counts %>% left_join(day_weights, by = "date") daily_counts_ipw$day_avg_sw[is.na(daily_counts_ipw$day_avg_sw)] <- 1 # no encounters that day ipw_irr <- model_generalized( dataframe = daily_counts_ipw, outcome_count = daily_counts_ipw$n_encounters_actual, exposure = daily_counts_ipw$extreme, intervention = daily_counts_ipw$post, weights = daily_counts_ipw$day_avg_sw ) ipw_irr ## [1] "0.96 (0.92, 1)" What to look for. Compare this IRR to the unweighted DiD estimate from Section 2.3. If they’re close, that’s evidence the compositional drift we simulated wasn’t actually biasing the unweighted estimate much. If they diverge, that tells you the population shift was doing some of the work you might otherwise have attributed to the intervention itself, exactly the ambiguity Hess et al. could not rule out for Ahmedabad because they had no individual-level data to weight on.

5 Bringing It Together (5 min)

5 Bringing It Together (5 min) true_effect_note <- "True simulated effect: ~36% reduction in heat-slope after 2016" comparison <- data.frame( Method = c("Case-crossover (informal pre vs post OR comparison)", "Difference-in-differences (unweighted, model_generalized())", "Difference-in-differences (IPW-weighted, model_generalized())"), Estimate = c( paste0(round(cc_summary$OR[cc_summary$period == "Pre (2010-2015)"], 2), " -> ", round(cc_summary$OR[cc_summary$period == "Post (2016-2020)"], 2)), did_overall_irr, ipw_irr ), What_it_controls_for = c( "Time-invariant confounders per person and stratum, not the citywide secular trend", "Shared secular trend and season, not compositional drift", "Shared secular trend, season, and measured compositional drift" ) ) print(comparison, row.names = FALSE) ## Method Estimate ## Case-crossover (informal pre vs post OR comparison) 1.65 -> 1.23 ## Difference-in-differences (unweighted, model_generalized()) 0.96 (0.92, 1) ## Difference-in-differences (IPW-weighted, model_generalized()) 0.96 (0.92, 1) ## What_it_controls_for ## Time-invariant confounders per person and stratum, not the citywide secular trend ## Shared secular trend and season, not compositional drift ## Shared secular trend, season, and measured compositional drift cat("\n", true_effect_note, "\n") ## ## True simulated effect: ~36% reduction in heat-slope after 2016 Discussion questions for the group: Which of these three estimates would you trust most, and why? Is your answer different if you imagine this were real data versus knowing, as we do here, the actual ground truth? The case-crossover comparison is the closest analogue in this workshop to what a simple pre/post design (like the core of the Ahmedabad HAP evaluation) can offer. What would you need to add to make it a genuine causal comparison? The IPW step only adjusts for compositional drift we measured and simulated on purpose. What are two or three plausible unmeasured confounders, in either Boston or Ahmedabad, that no amount of reweighting on the variables we have could fix? If you had to design a real evaluation of a new heat-adaptation program with only 2 years of pre-data and 2 years of post-data, which of these three designs would you prioritize building the data infrastructure for, and why?
